Title: The most efficient way to compute every natural number that can be written as the sum of two squares up to some bound

What is the most efficient way to compute every natural number that can be written as the sum of two squares up to some bound $N$?

The naive approach would consist of iterating $x,y$ over $(0, 1, \dots, \sqrt N)$ and, for each pair, adding $x^2+y^2$ to our list. This algorithm executes in $O(N)$ time, which is not too bad. However, it can be shown the numbers we wish to compute amount to approximately $\dfrac{bN}{\sqrt{\log N}}$ of the elements in $\{0, 1, \dots, N\}$, where $b\approx 0.76422\dots$ denotes the Landau–Ramanujan Constant. Thus, if we somehow avoid repetitions, one would accomplish a complexity of $O\left(\dfrac{N}{\sqrt{\log N}}\right)$. Is this possible?

It might be helpful to consider the sum of two squares theorem, which states a natural number can be written as the sum of two squares if, and only if, its prime factorization have no prime factor that is $3\pmod 4$ raised to an odd power. This could be used to compute such numbers with no repetition, but this would also involve computing the prime numbers up to $N$, which is itself less efficient than $O(N)$.

Title: Is there any other way to compute $ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x?$

Noticing that the integral can be expressed as a double integral, we have

$$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x &=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{(x+1)\left(x^2+1\right)} d x \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{x^2+1} \int_0^1 \cos ((x+1) y) d y d x \\ &=\int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\cos ((x+1) y)}{x^2+1} d x d y \\ &=\int_0^1 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos (x y) \cos y-\sin (x y) \sin y}{x^2+1} d x d y \\ & =\int_0^1\left(\cos y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos (x y)}{x^2+1} d x-\sin y \underbrace{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\sin (x y)}{x^2+1} d x}_{=0} \right) d y \end{aligned}\tag*{} $$

For the remaining integral, we use contour integration along anti-clockwise direction of the path $$\gamma=\gamma_{1} \cup \gamma_{2} \textrm{ where }  \gamma_{1}(t)=t+i 0(-R \leq t \leq R)  \textrm{ and } \gamma_{2}(t)=R e^{i t}  (0<t<\pi)$$
Let $R\rightarrow \infty$, then
$$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}  \frac{\cos (x y)}{x^2+1} d x=&\Re \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-x y i}}{x^2+1} d x \\ = & \Re \oint_\gamma \frac{e^{-z y i}}{z^2+1} d z\\=&\Re\left[2 \pi i\left(\frac{e^{-y}}{2 i}\right)\right] \\ = & \pi e^{-y}\end{aligned}\tag*{} $$

Plugging back with IBP yields
$$\displaystyle \boxed{ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x=\int_0^1 \pi e^{-y} \cos y d y=\frac{\pi}{2 e}(e+\sin 1-\cos 1)}\tag*{} $$

Is there any other way to compute $ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\sin (x+1)}{x^3+x^2+x+1} d x?$

There do not exist three integers $n$, $n+2$ and $n+4$, all of which are primes.

Proof:

Assume, to the contrary, that there exist three integers $n$, $n+2$ and $n+4$, all of which are primes. We can write $n$ as $3q$, $3q + 1$ or $3q + 2$, where $q\in\mathbb{Z}$. We
consider these three cases.

Case 1. $n = 3q$. Then $3 | n$ and so n is not prime. This is a contradiction.

Case 2. $n = 3q + 1$. Then $n + 2 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1)$. Since $q + 1$ is an integer,
$3 | (n + 2)$ and so $n + 2$ is not prime. Again, we have a contradiction.

Case 3. $n = 3q + 2$. Hence, we have $n + 4 = 3q + 6 = 3(q + 2)$. Since $q + 2$ is an
integer, $3 | (n + 4)$ and so $n + 4$ is not prime. This produces a contradiction.

But it’s obvious that when $n=3$ the cases hold since the sequence 3, 5 and 7 are prime. There is no restriction on $q$, so $q$ could be 0, 2 and 1 for $3q$, $3q+1$, $3q+2$ respectively. Was this an oversight by the author or am I mistaken?

Textbook: Mathematical Proofs: A Transition to Advanced Mathematics; Fourth Edition (pg. 324)
